Introduction to mcglmgraph

Source: vignettes/mcglmgraph-intro.Rmd
mcglmgraph-intro.Rmd

Overview

mcglmgraph extends Multivariate Covariance Generalized Linear Models (MCGLM) by structuring the residual between-response covariance Σb\Sigma_b with a graph. Three layers are available: the Gaussian graphical model (GGM), which parametrizes the precision matrix Kb=Σb−1K_b = \Sigma_b^{-1} so that its zeros are null partial correlations; the directed acyclic graph (DAG), which uses the modified Cholesky (LDL) decomposition under a fixed ordering of the responses; and the completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG), the equivalence class of DAGs that partial-correlation tests can identify, learned by structure-discovery routines. Numerically intensive operations run in C++ via RcppArmadillo.

Estimation proceeds in two stages. The first stage fits the marginal MCGLM (mean and dispersion blocks) and extracts the standardized Pearson residuals. The second stage forms their sample between-response covariance and fits the graph layer to this second-order object with the Pearson estimating functions of the MCGLM, without a joint likelihood. Graph edges therefore describe residual conditional association among responses, not raw marginal association. In the GGM layer, a missing edge means absence of second-order conditional association; it coincides with conditional independence only under joint normality of the analyzed residuals. In a Gaussian-copula model, that reading applies to a precision matrix fitted on the latent Gaussian scale; the Pearson-residual route does not perform that latent transformation.

library(mcglmgraph)

A worked example: recovering a chain graph

We simulate four responses whose true second-order conditional association graph is the chain 1−2−3−41 - 2 - 3 - 4, add a covariate to two of them, and fit the GGM layer.

set.seed(1)
n <- 300
K <- diag(4) * 2
K[1, 2] <- K[2, 1] <- -0.6
K[2, 3] <- K[3, 2] <- -0.6
K[3, 4] <- K[4, 3] <- -0.6
Y <- MASS::mvrnorm(n, rep(0, 4), solve(K))
x <- rnorm(n)
dat <- data.frame(y1 = Y[, 1] + 0.5 * x, y2 = Y[, 2],
                  y3 = Y[, 3], y4 = Y[, 4] - 0.3 * x, x = x)

fit <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x, y4 ~ x),
                   between_graph = mc_between_graph("ggm"), data = dat)
#> Automatic initial values selected.
fit
#> Multivariate Covariance GLM with graph-structured between-response covariance
#> Layer: GGM | responses: 4 | n: 300 | edges: 6
#> Between-response engine converged: TRUE (1 iterations)
#> 
#> Between-response covariance (Sigma_b):
#>         y1     y2      y3      y4
#> y1  0.9933 0.2606 -0.0033 -0.0142
#> y2  0.2606 0.9933  0.3174  0.0559
#> y3 -0.0033 0.3174  0.9933  0.2311
#> y4 -0.0142 0.0559  0.2311  0.9933
#> 
#> This is also a valid 'mcglm' object: use coef(), vcov(), gof(), ...

The partial correlations display the second-order conditional association structure. The precision matrix used in the simulation gives a partial correlation of 0.30 to each pair of adjacent responses and zero to the other pairs; the estimates for adjacent pairs are close to that value and those for non-adjacent pairs are close to zero.

round(mc_partial_cor(fit), 3)
#>        y1     y2     y3     y4
#> y1  1.000  0.278 -0.091 -0.009
#> y2  0.278  1.000  0.327 -0.016
#> y3 -0.091  0.327  1.000  0.225
#> y4 -0.009 -0.016  0.225  1.000

The regression coefficients are inherited from the marginal MCGLM fit. The graph layer leaves the mean target fixed and re-expresses the residual between-response covariance. The standard errors of the graph parameters are conditional on the first-stage fit unless a two-stage variance is requested (mc_vcov_graph(type = "two_stage")).

How much the first stage matters depends on the parameter. Suppose that the Pearson residual of each response is (y−μ)/𝜍(y - \mu)/\varsigma, with mean μ\mu and scale 𝜍\varsigma depending only on the first-stage parameters and the covariates, that the mean is correctly specified, and that the conditional covariance of the residuals given the covariates is the same Σb\Sigma_b for every unit. In the GGM layer, with a support that contains the nonzero off-diagonal entries of the true precision matrix, estimating the first stage then acts on the residual covariance, to first order, as a diagonal rescaling. Partial correlations and zeros of the precision matrix are invariant to such a rescaling, so the empirical (sandwich) variance of the partial correlations, mc_partial_cor_delta(variability = "empirical"), and the two-stage variance, variability = "two_stage", agree to first order, and so does the null distribution of the Wald test that an edge parameter is zero. The correction remains for the parameters that depend on the scale: the precision coefficients of the edges that are present and the diagonal terms. The model-based variance agrees with the two empirical forms only if, in addition, the working fourth moments are correct, as under normality. When the residual correlation changes with the covariates, as it can with count responses, the agreement is only approximate and the two-stage variance is the form to report.

Structure selection

In this sample, stepwise selection with BIC returns the three edges of the chain used in the simulation.

sel <- mc_graph_stepwise(fit, criterion = "bic")
sel$edges
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    2
#> [2,]    2    3
#> [3,]    3    4

The joint Wald test of the hypothesis that all edge parameters are zero rejects it here. The fit is also an mcglm object, so the mcglm methods (coef, vcov, gof, …) apply to it.

mc_test_independence(fit)
#> 
#>  Wald test of between-response conditional association
#> 
#> data:  GGM layer with 6 edges
#> X-squared = 60.215, df = 6, p-value = 4.071e-11
coef(fit)        # inherited mcglm method
#>      Estimates Parameters        Type Response
#> 1  -0.05565639     beta10        beta        1
#> 2   0.54683586     beta11        beta        1

#> 4  -0.02413884     beta21        beta        2
#> 5  -0.02278576     beta30        beta        3
#> 6   0.05732429     beta31        beta        3
#> 7  -0.02369288     beta40        beta        4
#> 8  -0.23584547     beta41        beta        4
#> 9   0.26238020      rho12 correlation       NA
#> 10 -0.00334519      rho13 correlation       NA

The DAG layer

The same data can be modeled with the directed acyclic graph layer, which uses the modified Cholesky decomposition and guarantees positive definiteness. In mcglmgraph, this is an ordered residual parametrization. A causal reading requires additional subject-matter assumptions, such as a defensible ordering, causal sufficiency and faithfulness. When no ordering is justified, the CPDAG layer (mc_graph_pipeline(), mc_ges()) learns the equivalence class instead.

fit_dag <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x, y4 ~ x),
                       between_graph = mc_between_graph("dag"), data = dat)
#> Automatic initial values selected.
mc_compute_criterion(fit_dag, c("aic", "bic"))
#>      aic      bic 
#> 3344.134 3381.172 
#> attr(,"criterion_status")
#> [1] "not_required"
#> attr(,"effective_dimension")
#> [1] NA
